excerpt: When a sprained ankle at work qualifies for workers' compensation, how to document it, and why insurers treat soft-tissue injuries with suspicion.

faqs.question: When does a sprained ankle count as a work injury?
faqs.answer: When it is work related. If the injury occurred on the job, or because of the job, it will generally be covered. Twisting your ankle on a walk at home is not covered; spraining it on an uneven factory floor at work generally is.

faqs.question: What is the threshold requirement for a workers' compensation claim?
faqs.answer: Work-relatedness. Whether the injury arose on the job or because of the job is the general test, and it is the question that has to be answered before the rest of the claim matters.

faqs.question: Why should I get medical treatment for a minor work injury?
faqs.answer: Because medical records are vital evidence. Treatment protects your recovery and documents when, where and how the injury happened. Skipping care leaves you without the documentation a claim depends on.

faqs.question: Should I report a minor injury to my employer?
faqs.answer: Yes. If you believe the injury may be work related, report it as soon as possible after it happens. Minor injuries sometimes turn out to be more serious, and a late report gives the insurer room to dispute the connection to work.

faqs.question: Does workers' compensation cover occupational illnesses too?
faqs.answer: Yes. The same work-relatedness test covers conditions that develop because of the job over time, not only single accidents. Those claims turn on connecting the condition to your work conditions rather than to one event.
